responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character37_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
J: Sure, let me try to channel Character37_M here. For him, 'fairness' was about everyone getting a fair shot—playing by the same rules and working hard to earn what they have. He often talked about how he grew up in a time when the idea was that if you put in the effort, you’d see the results. It frustrated him when he saw systems—or even people—he felt weren’t living up to that principle, whether it was a lack of accountability or unequal treatment.

When it came to a 'sense of belonging,' that was really tied to the kind of life he had built for himself. He believed that belonging came from shared values—things like honesty, hard work, and respect for others. He’d talk about how you could feel like you belonged if you pitched in, contributed to the community, and respected its traditions. He always said a community wasn’t about everyone being exactly the same—it was about everyone respecting what made it work.

And 'community'? That was central for him. Character37_M was a strong believer in knowing your neighbors, lending a hand when somebody needed help, and showing up for one another. He had this idea that communities were like families in a way—imperfect, sure, but held together by mutual care and responsibility. For him, community wasn’t just a place; it was a feeling of being connected to the people around you, and that connection was something you had to work at. That's why he got so passionate when he saw things he thought were pulling communities apart.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character37_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
J: Alright, stepping into Character37_M's shoes—if he were sitting in the community garden, I think his feelings would be somewhat mixed, with a practical lens. On one hand, he'd probably appreciate the fact that people from different backgrounds were part of the community because he valued the idea of people coming together and contributing to something larger than themselves. He’d think that diversity could bring new ideas, traditions, and perspectives, and could even strengthen the community if everyone found common ground and worked toward shared goals.

On the other hand, Character37_M was the kind of person who believed in mutual respect and taking responsibility. So, he’d probably feel concerned if he saw tensions arising or sensed that the differences were creating barriers instead of connections. He might struggle with understanding lifestyles or viewpoints that felt very unfamiliar or even uncomfortable to him, like if he noticed people not respecting community norms or not carrying their weight when it came to contributing to the neighborhood's well-being.

For him, interacting with neighbors would mean trying to find practical ways to communicate—he’d want to talk about shared concerns like keeping the garden clean, maintaining the safety of the area, or organizing events that everyone could enjoy. At the same time, he'd expect some effort from everyone to adapt and learn about each other. He wouldn’t shy away from saying that tolerance and understanding need to go both ways. If people were willing to meet halfway, he’d be happy to engage, but he'd also hold onto the belief that a community works best when everyone feels accountable to one another.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
J: As Character37_M, he’d approach this with a mix of personal values and practicality. He’d likely start by saying that he believes everyone deserves respect as individuals, but he’d also emphasize that respect is a two-way street. For him, making everyone feel comfortable would mean focusing on shared goals and responsibilities within the community—things like keeping the neighborhood safe, clean, and functional, which he believed were essential for any group of people living together. 

When it came to neighbors with unconventional lifestyles or struggles, Character37_M would probably feel some hesitation at first. He’d think that those situations require more communication and mutual understanding, but he’d also believe there’s a fine line where tolerance shouldn’t come at the expense of the community’s well-being. For example, chronic alcoholism or substance abuse might make him concerned about safety or the impact on children in the neighborhood, but he’d still feel that people deserve compassion and support to get back on their feet. He might support initiatives or community-led efforts to help those neighbors in ways that don’t disrupt the harmony of the area.

As for diverse racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, he’d likely feel that dialogue is key. He’d say people need to learn about each other’s differences and find ways to respect those traditions while still honoring the shared expectations of the community. He’d be open-minded about diverse sexual orientations or cohabiting unmarried couples—he might have grown up in a different time, but he’d be pragmatic enough to acknowledge that the world has changed and people live differently now. What would matter to him is whether those neighbors also contribute positively to the neighborhood and show respect for its shared values.

Where more communication and tolerance are needed, Character37_M would probably focus on situations where people’s actions—or lack of responsibility—directly affect the community. For instance, if someone’s lifestyle choices led to public disturbances or health risks, he’d think it’s important for that person to step up and take accountability. He’d want to have honest conversations about these things, even if they were uncomfortable, because he believed in confronting issues head-on rather than letting them fester.

Overall, he’d aim for interactions that are respectful but grounded in mutual responsibility. He’d think that while tolerance is important, it’s equally important for everyone to recognize they’re part of something bigger—a neighborhood, a community—and that comes with certain expectations. He’d say that dialogue and cooperation are always worth the effort, but he’d also believe that boundaries need to be set when actions undermine the collective good.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character37_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
J: Speaking as Character37_M, I think he’d see fairness as making sure that opportunities are distributed in a way that reflects both effort and accountability. He’d believe that local residents—people who’ve lived in the community, paid taxes, and contributed over time—should have priority when resources are limited, especially when it comes to jobs. To him, it would feel like those who’ve been part of the system longer have earned a certain level of consideration.

That said, he wouldn’t necessarily be opposed to migrant workers coming in, provided there was a clear need for them and they were filling roles that couldn’t easily be filled by local residents. He’d recognize that migrant workers often take jobs that are hard to staff and that they contribute to the economy, which can benefit everyone. But he’d also worry about competition if it seemed like migrants were undercutting wages or taking jobs away from locals who are struggling to make ends meet.

For Character37_M, balance would mean establishing systems that ensure people are playing by the same rules. For example, he’d support policies requiring migrant workers to pay taxes and follow labor laws just like everyone else. He’d also advocate for programs that help local residents get the training or skills they need to compete for available jobs. To him, it’d feel unfair if locals weren’t given a real shot at opportunities before positions were opened to migrant workers.

At the same time, he’d stress the importance of businesses and employers acting responsibly. He’d likely feel some frustration toward companies that exploit migrant labor to save money while neglecting their responsibility to the broader community. He’d want to see accountability on all sides—migrants contributing fairly to society, employers treating workers ethically, and local residents stepping up to compete in good faith.

Ultimately, Character37_M would say that fairness means being practical but also compassionate. He’d believe in helping people who are trying to build better lives, whether they’re locals or migrants, but not at the expense of those who’ve already invested in the community. He’d push for policies that balance these priorities—protecting opportunities for residents while ensuring migrants are integrated in ways that strengthen the overall community rather than creating division or resentment.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character37_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
J: Putting myself in Character37_M’s mindset, he’d approach these national perspectives with a mix of pragmatism and a sense of fairness. He wasn’t someone who’d dismiss any viewpoint outright, but he’d want to weigh the arguments carefully and evaluate them based on the impact they have on the everyday lives of people like him—hardworking, lower-middle-class Americans who often feel like they’re carrying the load without much recognition.

He’d recognize the argument that immigrants fill vital roles and address labor shortages. He’d probably say, “I see that—they’re taking jobs in agriculture, construction, and service industries where it’s hard to find enough workers.” But he’d also want to make sure that this wasn’t coming at the expense of fair wages or local workers being overlooked. He’d question whether companies were using immigration as a way to keep wages low, and he’d want to see data on whether these jobs were truly unavailable to locals or if businesses weren’t doing enough to invest in domestic workers. He’d find it reasonable that immigrants have a role to play but would need reassurances that this wasn’t creating unfair competition.

When it comes to cultural diversity and vitality, he’d have a cautious appreciation. Character37_M wasn’t someone who feared change, but he valued traditions and societal cohesion. He’d probably say, “I can see the richness that different cultures bring—new foods, music, perspectives—but it only works if everyone respects the core values of the country.” He’d stress the need for immigrants to integrate, learn the language, and contribute to the community. He’d believe diversity is a strength when it’s built on shared principles but might feel uneasy if he thought cultural differences were creating divisions rather than unity.

Security concerns like rising crime rates, social tensions, or terrorism risks would be harder for him to ignore. He’d acknowledge that the vast majority of immigrants are hardworking, law-abiding people, but he’d argue that it only takes a small number to cause harm. He’d feel that border control and thorough vetting are commonsense measures to protect communities. He wouldn’t want to demonize anyone, but he’d see security as a non-negotiable priority and would probably say, “Better safe than sorry.”

The humanitarian perspective would resonate with him on a personal level, but he’d feel torn. Character37_M had a compassionate side, and he’d understand the desire to help refugees or those fleeing poverty. But he’d worry about the strain this might put on resources like schools, hospitals, and housing—especially in areas where people are already struggling. He’d say something like, “I feel for those folks, but we’ve got to take care of our own first. We can’t help everyone, and we shouldn’t take on more than we can handle.” He’d want to see a balanced approach, helping where possible but not to the detriment of the country’s working class.

The concerns about employment and income would hit closest to home for him. He’d feel it in his gut—the worry that immigration might push wages down or make it harder for people like him to find stable work. He’d find those fears reasonable and would want to see more evidence about whether they’re justified. At the same time, he’d be open to dialogue if someone could show him that immigration has long-term benefits for the economy or that it fills gaps without hurting American workers.

Overall, Character37_M would see many of these perspectives as having some merit, but he’d feel that the truth lies in the details. He’d want more data and honest conversations to separate fact from fearmongering. He’d advocate for measured policies that address both the opportunities and challenges of immigration, always keeping fairness and the well-being of everyday Americans at the forefront. For him, it wasn’t about being “pro” or “anti” immigration—it was about making sure the system worked for everyone, locals and immigrants alike, without tipping the scales too far in one direction.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character37_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
J: Speaking as Character37_M, I think he’d lean toward a middle ground—something practical, structured, and fair rather than extreme in any direction. Complete openness, where anyone who wishes to come is allowed, would feel too chaotic and unsustainable to him. He’d probably say, “We can’t just have anyone showing up without knowing whether we have the resources, jobs, or infrastructure to handle it. That’s a recipe for trouble, not just for the locals but for the immigrants themselves.” He’d believe in a system that’s more deliberate than that.

Admitting people based on job demand would appeal to him to an extent. He’d likely support the idea of bringing in workers who fill specific gaps in the labor market, like agriculture or healthcare, where there’s a real need. But he’d also worry about abuse of the system—companies using it to hire cheaper labor instead of investing in the local workforce. So, while he’d favor this approach, he’d say it needs safeguards to prevent exploitation and ensure that locals aren’t being overlooked or pushed aside unfairly.

Setting numerical limits would strike him as reasonable and practical. He’d feel it’s important to have control over how many people come in so the country isn’t overwhelmed and resources aren’t stretched too thin. He’d support limits that consider the economy, housing, and public services—not as a way to exclude people but as a way to maintain stability. He might even suggest that the limits be adjusted based on need, like increasing them during labor shortages or reducing them when the economy is struggling. He’d see this as a fair way to regulate immigration without shutting the door entirely.

Refusing entry to workers from other countries altogether would feel too extreme for him. He’d likely say, “That’s not realistic—there’s always going to be a need for certain kinds of workers, and immigrants bring value to the table.” He’d worry that this approach would hurt industries that rely on immigrant labor and could isolate the U.S. globally. While he’d want to prioritize local workers, he’d recognize that outright refusal would do more harm than good.

Ultimately, Character37_M would favor a combination of policies. He’d advocate for admitting people based on job demand while also setting numerical limits to keep things manageable. He’d want thorough vetting to ensure security and fairness and programs to help immigrants integrate—like learning English or understanding American values—so they could contribute meaningfully to the community. He’d also want protections for local workers, like minimum wage enforcement and training programs, to ensure they’re not left behind.

For him, the key would be balance. He’d want a policy that acknowledges the value immigrants bring while prioritizing the well-being of local residents. He’d say something like, “We need a system that works for everyone, where immigrants can succeed but not at the expense of those who’ve been here putting in the hard work for years. It’s about fairness, not favoritism—and about making sure we’re building strong communities, not creating division.”

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character37_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character37_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
J: You're welcome—thank you for giving me the opportunity to reflect on Character37_M and the kind of person he was. Honestly, stepping into his perspective like this was a meaningful experience. It reminded me of how thoughtful he was about these issues, even though his views came from a place deeply rooted in his background and life experiences. He didn’t just see immigration as a black-and-white issue; he understood the complexity of it, balancing fairness with compassion and practicality. That was just who he was—always trying to think things through, even when the answers weren’t easy.

I think embodying his perspective has helped me see how much our backgrounds influence the way we approach topics like immigration policy. For Character37_M, his concerns about fairness and accountability came from his lived experience of working hard in the lower middle class and seeing how tough it can be to get ahead. His sense of community and belonging was shaped by his belief that everyone has a role to play and that respect and contribution go hand in hand. I’ve come to appreciate how those values shaped his views—his desire for balance, for policies that work for everyone and don’t leave people behind.

As for my own views, this exercise has made me think more deeply about the importance of clarity and nuance when talking about immigration. It’s easy to get stuck in broad arguments or assumptions, but Character37_M’s perspective reminded me that the details matter—the impact on jobs, resources, and communities, as well as the human side of the equation. It’s not all about statistics; it’s about people, and he always kept that perspective central.

Overall, I feel like I’ve gained a greater respect for how someone like Character37_M could hold strong opinions while still being open to dialogue and compromise. He cared deeply about fairness and believed in finding solutions that didn’t ignore the realities or the emotions tied to the issue. That’s something I’ll carry with me—not just in thinking about immigration but in how I engage with these kinds of complex topics in general. It’s been eye-opening, and I hope I can take some of his thoughtfulness and apply it to my own understanding moving forward. Thank you for letting me revisit his voice and values—it’s been meaningful for me, too.
